True-up asks the owner before it rewrites an edited suite file only when git tracks the edit, so an edit to a suite file that git does not track is overwritten with no question and no archive copy. The owner never gets to turn the upgrade down, and the edit is gone.

An untracked file's edit is held in no commit. [story:turn-down-a-destructive-true-up](.ok-planner/design/stories/turn-down-a-destructive-true-up.md) promises the owner a way to turn down an upgrade that would rewrite their files.

problem:
True-up looks for a person's edits to the files the suite wrote only in git's diff, which never lists a file git does not track. So true-up overwrites an edited file git does not track with no question to the owner and no archive copy, and the edit is lost.

True-up is the suite's upgrade pass. It rewrites each suite-owned file, one the suite writes and stamps with its version, to the new release's text. Rewriting a file a person edited is destructive. Before a destructive plan runs, the front door, `/ok`, asks the owner once, and true-up copies the file into the archive. [decision:true-up-asks-once-before-destructive-steps](.ok-planner/design/decisions/true-up-asks-once-before-destructive-steps.md) exempts only "a suite-owned file that still carries its stamp or its fixed content and holds no uncommitted or staged-only change", because "a suite-owned file whose every change git holds in a commit destroys nothing git cannot restore". [story:turn-down-a-destructive-true-up](.ok-planner/design/stories/turn-down-a-destructive-true-up.md) promises the owner a way to turn down an upgrade that rewrites their files.

problem:
`review drives --confirm` files no confirm driver for a story whose drive defect a verifier marked a duplicate of another defect, so `/converge` reports the story fixed with no drive to show it holds.

In a `/converge` run, a driver uses the product as a user would and files a defect with `source: drive`. After the defect's fix is verified, `review drives --confirm` files a confirm driver that tries the story again. The review tool picks those defects in [review:unconfirmed_drive_defects](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1388): it keeps a defect only where its state is `verified` and its `source` is `drive`. A verifier that accepts a drive defect as a duplicate (`same_as`) of another defect leaves the drive defect at state `duplicate` and verifies the other one. The other defect usually came from the sprint review or an analysis hunt, so it fails the `source` test, and the drive defect fails the state test. Neither is confirmed.

The linescout platform project met this on 2026-10-23: a driver found that renaming a device answers 500 under the project's rename-a-device story. The verifier marked that defect a duplicate of one the sprint review found and verified the review's fix. No confirm driver tried the rename again. The filter reads the same in ok-planner v31.0.0.

The harm falls under accept-list entry A9: the run reports a story fixed when no drive shows the story holds.

problem:
Today `/plan-sprint` re-plans a tested story whenever a sprint's work changes that story's code, but it re-plans the runtime scenarios only when the owner takes the optional runtime offer at Frame. The ruling decides whether a sprint that changes a part must also re-plan that part's runtime scenarios.

A runtime scenario checks that the product survives a failure of one part, such as a restart, a missing setting, or bad data. [decision:scenario-list-decided-once](.ok-planner/design/decisions/scenario-list-decided-once.md) states for stories: "A sprint must re-plan each tested story whose behavior its work changes, whether or not the story's text changes", with the rationale "a required re-plan follows the code a sprint changes, not the story's file". For runtime parts it says only "The runtime parts and the classes that apply to each are part of the same list." [decision:testing-runs-inside-the-sprint](.ok-planner/design/decisions/testing-runs-inside-the-sprint.md) lists "runtime scenarios" among the groups the owner may take. No decision gives a reason for the difference. In the code, `tests groups --replan` touches each tested story the code planner lists, and the runtime planner runs only under `--take runtime` ([plan-sprint](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/SKILL.md), [tests](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests)).

Had the owner declined the offer, no planner would have re-sorted them; they would fail at certification, whose fixers assume a failing test is right and work to restore the removed behavior. The owner found the offer confusing: an optional choice, while testing is on, for tests the sprint's own work breaks. The suite's word "runtime" also collided with the project's own concept of a device runtime.

The ruling decides whether planning re-plans the runtime scenarios a sprint's work reaches without the owner's choice.

`tests tasks --stage write` refuses to file anything when a test task it must refile waits, through its copied `after` list, on an earlier test task that also closed `blocked`. That earlier task is refiled in the same pass, so the refusal is false, and the sprint's execution brief makes it a genuine blocker that stops the run.

A sprint's write stage chains test tasks that share a test file with `after`. problem:
A sprint run that writes its stop record never ends the /goal that started it. The goal stays open, and its stop hook sends the session back to work on every turn until the owner runs /goal clear.

The suite assumes the goal checker can end a goal unmet. It cannot. The checker is a separate model that reads the session and answers one question: is the condition met? The harness clears the goal only on a yes, or on /goal clear. The suite's wording, in step 1 of the sprint template's "How to execute this sprint" (plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/sprint-document.md, line 110 onward), says "The goal also ends, unmet, when that command prints SPRINT STOPPED". The review script's stopped_verdict (plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review, line 2174) prints "This ends the goal for this sprint file". Neither sentence makes the condition true, so the checker answers no.

Step 1 also hangs the stop clause on the executor's first message. The executor must restate it in exact words. Nothing checks that it did, and a long run's context compaction can drop that message.

The linescout platform project met this on 2026-11-09 in sprint 2026-11-08-cli-as-client, under ok-planner v31.0.0. The executor never stated the stop condition. The run stopped on a genuine blocker, the write-stage-refuses-chained-blocked-refiles issue. review certified printed SPRINT STOPPED and "This ends the goal for this sprint file". The checker then held the goal open through ten stop-hook rounds. Its first round said "The stop record ends the goal unmet" and blocked anyway. Later rounds said "The goal condition requires the sprint to reach SPRINT COMPLETE." The owner cleared the goal by hand.

Sites: sprint-document.md step 1 and its step 11 stop wording; review's stopped_verdict; the same wording in docs, ok-planner-CLAUDE.md, ok-planner-cheatsheet.md, _sprint/shared.md, and plan-docs/doc-sprint-document.md.

problem:
A sprint's write stage makes each test task wait on the support tasks for the files its scenario's `support` list names, and on no others. The test planner writes that list by hand, from the files the test uses directly. It does not follow imports from one support file to another, or through the shared conftest files every test loads. So a test task can start while a support file it imports still holds code the sprint deleted. The test fails to load, records a `support` item, and closes `blocked`, even though a support task for that file is already filed and will fix it minutes later.

Sites: plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/tests-story.md, the step that names a new or rewritten test's support files (line 141); plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests, the write stage that files each test task "after the support tasks for its files".

messages.text:
A second project's sprint points the other way, and toward option B.

The zonebase project certified sprint 2026-11-08-production-stack under `testing.enabled: on` (ok-planner v31.0.0). That sprint's deltas added all 16 of the project's stories, so its drive and option B's drive are the same set. The drive ran 18 drive tasks, one per story plus 2 confirms. It used about 54M processed tokens, about 2% of execution's estimated 2.4B. It found 2 verified defects in files the sprint changed, and the merge declined a third. The suite passed 347 tests at the end, and both stories had passing tests.

- The bbox branch of GET /v1/changes (backend/src/features/changes-feed/list-by-bbox.ts::handleListByBbox) reads only bbox, page, and pageSize, so it drops status and city. `?bbox=...&status=proposed` lists adopted cases too, and `?city=nowhere&bbox=...` answers 200 where `?city=nowhere` alone answers 400. The story has 17 tests, among them a bbox test and a status-filter test. No test combines the two.
- The MCP servers (backend/src/entrypoints/agent-mcp-server.ts::main and mcp-server.ts::main) hand every client's POST to one stateless transport. The SDK keys open responses by bare request id, so two clients that call at once with the same id lose one reply. The driver sent two record_ordinance_fetch_plan calls 50 ms apart, and one never answered. The story has 23 tests, and each makes one call at a time.

Both are the gap the linescout sweep found: no scenario names the outcome that broke. Here the drive found them inside the sprint, in its own change, for a small share of the cost. The two projects differ mainly in story count: linescout drove 113 stories and zonebase 16. So the drive's cost follows the stories it takes, and its yield follows how new they are. Option B keeps the drive on new and amended stories, where this sprint shows it pays. Option A would have shipped both defects.
Both. A standalone drive skill that a user can run to drive every story, and that sprint certification uses to drive only the sprint's new or changed stories.

The whole-product drive runs as `/converge drive` on the owner's cadence, as its own step, and each drive failure in a tested story is also recorded as a scenario gap for the next sprint's test planning.

options.label: B

problem:
Sprint certification drives every story of the project in every sprint, even where testing is on and the suite already covers the sprint's change, so each sprint pays for a whole-product drive that finds little in the change it certifies. `review certified` fails any sprint whose certification run filed no driver, so a project cannot move the drive out of the sprint on its own.

In `sprint` mode, [converge's SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L15) runs "a drive of every story" beside the review, the checks, and, where `testing.enabled` is `on` or `frozen`, the suite. [scripts/review](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1995) then refuses the certification where the run's ledger holds no `drive` task: "the drive did not run in <ledger>".

The linescout platform project measured one sprint under `testing.enabled: on` (2026-11-08-cli-as-client, ok-planner v31.0.0). The drive round ran 114 drive tasks and used 28% of the sprint's token cost, more than any other part. It found no defect in the sprint's change. The review passes found 7, for about 2.5% of the cost, and the suite found 24, passing 1,090 tests at the end. The suite covers 111 of the project's 113 stories. The drive's 28 failed or stuck checks went three ways: 15 repeated issues already in the intake, 7 were not owed, and 6 became new issues outside the sprint's change. 2 of those 6 are real defects no scenario names.

So the drive did two jobs. As certification of the sprint's change, it repeated the suite. As a sweep of the whole product, it found outcomes the scenario list never named. That sweep has value, but it need not run inside every sprint.

problem:
Every test-stage agent runs under the ok-opus profile, which inherits every tool but Agent and loads every unscoped rules file, so each of hundreds of short agents rereads a starting context sized for build and fix agents on every request.

[agents/ok-opus.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/agents/ok-opus.md) sets `disallowedTools: Agent` and no `tools` list, so its agents inherit the session's built-in and MCP tools. It does not set `omitClaudeMd`, so every `.claude/rules/*.md` file without `paths` loads. The test prompt reaches the agent only in the output of `tasks claim`, after the cached prefix: [skills/converge/prompts/test-write.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/test-write.md) is 7,987 characters, and [test-verify.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/test-verify.md) is 8,084.

The linescout platform project measured one sprint under `testing.enabled: on` (2026-11-08-cli-as-client, ok-planner v31.0.0, Claude Code 2.1.322). The sprint ran 331 test-write agents and 332 verify agents, 713 test-stage agents in all. Each test-write agent's first request read a cached prefix of 69,550 tokens, and every later request read it again: 12.9 requests on average. That prefix held about 106,000 characters of rules files, 71,000 of them the four suite cheatsheets. Every agent also gets a skill listing, one entry with its description for each of the session's skills; the test agent's listing ran 29,734 characters for 52 skills, 8,187 of them the project's ten skills, every one of which opens "ONLY activated by explicit /... slash command". Each agent's claim output, mostly the prompt, came to about 6,500 tokens written to cache per agent, since it sits after the shared prefix.

Claude Code's subagent frontmatter offers two levers. `tools` names the only tools a subagent gets. `omitClaudeMd: true` (Claude Code 2.1.271 and later) starts a subagent without the user, project, and local CLAUDE.md files and unscoped rules; rules with `paths` still load when the agent reads or edits a matching file. A profile's body is its system prompt, so a prompt placed there joins the cached prefix every agent of the profile shares.

The project measured the levers with four probe subagents, each defined with `claude --agents` in a headless session in the project folder, each replying one word. The first request's whole input came to:

- `disallowedTools: Agent`, as ok-opus sets: 51,289 tokens, with a 25,826-character skill listing, 133 deferred tool names, and 92,258 characters of rules files.
- `disallowedTools: Agent, Skill`: 42,056 tokens. Denying the Skill tool drops the skill listing, about 9,200 tokens.
- `tools: Bash, Read, Edit, Write`: 36,870 tokens. The allowlist drops the skill listing and the deferred tool names.
- the same `tools` and `omitClaudeMd: true`: 5,041 tokens. No rules file loads.

So the rules files are about 31,800 tokens of the floor, and the skill listing and deferred tools about 14,400. A lean agent with no rules loses the rules a test agent needs, such as the testing standard's ambient copy and the comment rule, and every project rule, such as a rule that binds every run of the project's CLI; those must reach it through path-scoped rules on the test paths or through its prompt.

Its body carries the rules sections a test agent needs, generated by true-up from the cheatsheet source. The role prompts stay in the claim output, not the profile body. See the ruling on vendored-profiles-start-from-an-unshrunk-context.

problem:
True-up writes the four suite cheatsheets under `.claude/rules/` with no `paths` frontmatter, so Claude Code loads all of them into every session and every subagent, whatever the agent works on. The suite also gives a project no advice to scope its own rules, so a project rule that binds one step of one skill loads into every agent too.

[admin/true-up](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/true-up#L205) materializes `scripts/ok-planner-cheatsheet.md` (28,122 characters), `scripts/ok-cheatsheet.md` (5,175), `docs/plumbline-cheatsheet.md` (22,676), and `docs/plumbline-coding.md` (15,395) as unscoped rules. Much of that text binds one kind of work: the coding rules bind agents that change code; the Tests section binds test work; the Documentation section binds documentation sprints; the lifecycle text binds the session that plans or executes.

Claude Code reads a `paths` list in a rule's frontmatter. A rule with `paths` loads only when the agent uses Read, Write, or Edit on a matching file, or views one with a single-file `cat` or `head`. Two limits apply: invoking a skill through the Skill tool, or a script reading a file, loads no scoped rule; and a rule that loads on demand has a per-file size limit, past which the agent sees only its start.

The linescout platform project measured one sprint under `testing.enabled: on` (2026-11-08-cli-as-client, ok-planner v31.0.0, Claude Code 2.1.322). Every agent's cached prefix held about 106,000 characters of rules, which each agent reread on every request; the project's test-stage agents alone made 8,846 requests. The project scoped four of its own rules by path: the drain-window rule to `.claude/skills/_tasks/drain.md`, the duplicate-drive confirm rule to `.claude/skills/converge/**` and the drain loop, the skill-prohibitions rule to `.claude/**/*.md`, and the error-helper rule to its code folders.

ruling.text: Keep the four cheatsheets unscoped and whole for now; path-scoping waits for a later sprint and measurement. The context savings come from the ruling on vendored-profiles-start-from-an-unshrunk-context: tool lists without the Skill tool, shorter skill descriptions, and lean profiles that carry their rules in the profile body.

title: The suite loads its four cheatsheets whole into every agent, and gives projects no advice to scope their own rules by path

messages.text: Four changes, and no change to how the rules files load. (1) The four suite cheatsheets stay unscoped and whole; the session and the general ok-opus build and fix agents keep loading every rule. (2) Each profile names a tools list with only the tools its jobs use and leaves out the Skill tool, so no agent gets the skill list or the deferred tool names. (3) Shorten the suite's skill descriptions to what a session needs to know: each skill runs only on its explicit slash command. Recommend claudeMdExcludes for an ancestor folder's CLAUDE.md. (4) Add lean specialized profiles, starting with ok-test for the test stages' support, test, verify, and speed roles, with omitClaudeMd: true and a tools list; each profile's body, its system prompt, which compaction keeps, carries the rules sections its jobs need, generated by true-up from the cheatsheet source so no second copy is kept by hand. Path-scoping the cheatsheets waits for a later sprint and measurement.

options.label: A
options.text: Shrink every profile's start and keep the task-tracker model. (1) Scope the suite's rules by path, and recommend `paths` for project rules. (2) Give each profile, or each role that needs a different tool set, a `tools` list naming only the tools its jobs use, leaving out the Skill tool, so no agent gets the skill list: a driver keeps the browser tools, and a test writer gets Bash, Read, Edit, Write, Grep, and Glob. (3) Shorten the suite's skill descriptions to what tells a session when to run the skill. (4) Recommend `claudeMdExcludes` for an ancestor folder's CLAUDE.md, and use `omitClaudeMd: true` on a profile that takes every rule it needs by path or from its prompt. (5) Keep each profile's first message identical and free of task text, so whatever loads stays one cached prefix per profile; where a role's prompt is the same for every agent, put it in the profile's body so it joins that prefix.

options.label: B
options.text: Take steps (2) and (5) only: the tool lists and the cached prefix, which change no rule text.

problem:
The suite's three agent profiles start every agent from the session's whole instruction set, so each of the hundreds of short agents a sprint runs rereads, on every request, rules, skill descriptions, and CLAUDE.md files its job never uses. The task-tracker model keeps that start cheap to reread, because every agent of one profile sends one identical first message and so shares one cached prefix. The suite can keep that model and shrink what the prefix holds.

[agents/ok-opus.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/agents/ok-opus.md), [agents/ok-haiku.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/agents/ok-haiku.md), and [agents/ok-review.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/agents/ok-review.md) set no `tools` list, so their agents inherit every built-in and MCP tool, and every tool brings the skill list and the names of the tools that load on request. True-up writes the suite's four cheatsheets with no `paths` frontmatter, so they load into every agent. The suite says nothing about CLAUDE.md files, so an ancestor folder's CLAUDE.md loads into every agent of a project nested in a larger repository.

The linescout platform project measured one sprint (2026-11-08-cli-as-client, ok-planner v31.0.0, Claude Code 2.1.322). 1,820 agents ran. A test agent's first request read a cached prefix of 69,550 tokens, and every later request read it again. Four probe subagents, defined with `claude --agents` in the project folder, put the parts of that floor at:

- rules files and CLAUDE.md files: about 31,800 tokens (92,258 characters), dropped by `omitClaudeMd: true`;
- the skill list and the tool names that load on request: about 14,400 tokens, dropped by a `tools` list that leaves out the Skill tool; denying the Skill tool alone drops the skill list, about 9,200 tokens;
- what remains with both: 5,041 tokens.

The skill list ran 29,734 characters for 52 skills. The suite's own skill descriptions are among the longest, 1,433 to 1,553 characters for `plan-sprint`, `converge`, and `triage-issues`, though each opens "ONLY activated by explicit /... slash command" and no agent invokes one.

Three issues filed beside this one carry parts of it in detail: `rules-files-load-whole-into-every-agent` (scope the suite's rules by path), `test-stage-agents-start-from-the-full-opus-context` (a lean test profile), and `test-tasks-file-one-agent-per-scenario` (one test agent per story). The project took two steps of its own: it scoped four project rules by path, and set `claudeMdExcludes` in `.claude/settings.json` to skip the parent repository's CLAUDE.md, which a project rule already told every agent to ignore.

messages.text: A, fix the three bugs, with part 4 changed. (1) Result lines carry started and ended on the suite command's clock, and schedule_failures compares those; a line without them falls back to today's check. (2) The preflight and /ok-setup's runner check run the suite command over two tests of one held group and check the order of their lines, run testing.setup twice in a row on a running stack, and run it once beside resources it did not create. (3) A round whose failures are only schedule pairs or a failed setup files no speed step. (4) Performance improves opportunistically: certification applies a product-slow fix only when another whole-suite round will run anyway. Once a round passes with nothing left to fix, no perf fix lands after it; each remaining product-slow verdict is filed as an issue for the next sprint, which runs the full suite anyway.

options.label: A
options.text: Prevent each fault before or inside the round that would meet it. (1) The result line carries `started` and `ended` on the suite command's own clock, and `schedule_failures` compares those, not arrival less seconds; a line without them falls back to today's check. (2) The preflight, and `/ok-setup`'s runner check, run the suite command over two tests of one held group and check the order of their lines, run `testing.setup` twice in a row on a running stack, and run it once beside a container outside the stack on the same network. (3) A round whose failures are only schedule pairs or a failed setup files no speed step. (4) Certification fixes every product-slow verdict before it runs the round it means to close on.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the checks as they are and document the contracts: the suite command's guide names streamed result lines and held-group order, and the setup's guide names re-runs on a running stack and foreign containers on the network. Add a tolerance of `testing.schedule_slack` seconds to `schedule_failures`, and no other change.

problem:
Sprint certification reopens its loop on every failed whole-suite round, and three kinds of round fail where neither the product nor a test is at fault: the schedule check reads timing noise as two tests running together, a setup meets a stack or network it did not expect, and a product-slow fix lands after the round that would have closed the run. Each such round costs another whole-suite round, and a round the schedule check fails also files a speed step. Nothing before the sprint checks the project's suite command or setup for these faults, so certification finds them one round at a time.

The zonebase project's sprint 2026-11-08-production-stack (ok-planner v31.0.0, `testing.enabled: on`, schedule `groups-one-at-a-time`, 347 tests) ran 7 whole-suite rounds. The design needs 2: the first, and one that passes after the last change. Each round took 2 to 4 minutes; the cost lay in what the 5 extra rounds set off.

1. **The schedule check reads timing noise as overlap.** [scripts/tests](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L2797) `schedule_failures` takes each test's start as its result line's arrival less the seconds the line reports, so it subtracts a time on the suite command's clock from a time on the tool's clock. Two rounds in which every test passed failed on that check alone:
   - Round 984: the project's runner, vitest named runs, wrote a file's result lines together when the file ended. Held tests of one file arrived together, so each one's derived start fell before the arrival of the test ahead of it, and the check found 7 pairs. A support task made the runner stream each result as its test settled.
   - Round 1002: the check found 3 more pairs from overlaps of a few milliseconds. One pair: `scheduled-refresh--changed-layer-reaches-customers` from 59.48 s to 68.747 s and `scheduled-refresh--ordinance-amendment-refetched` from 68.742 s, an overlap of 5 ms. A second support task capped each line's seconds so no derived start precedes the previous line's arrival. That cap bends the reported seconds to fit the check.
   The round-1002 failure also filed a speed step of 10 speed tasks, as converge's SKILL.md step 3a.2 files one for any failed round. 10 breaches took 18 `--only` reruns to confirm.
2. **Setup fails against a stack in a state it did not expect.** [ok-setup's SKILL.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/ok-setup/SKILL.md#L62) says `testing.setup` "must be safe to run again", and nothing checks it. Round 946: `docker compose up --wait` re-created a running stack, and a container lost its network ("container ... is not connected to the network zonebase_default"). Round 1006: two containers the owner started before the sprint held the same network, and the run stopped 1h11m for the owner's word. Each failed setup failed every test and cost a round. Single-test confirm reruns started 8 at a time from a stopped stack collided in setup the same way: 21 of 26 ran again one at a time.
3. **A product-slow fix lands after the closing round.** The linescout platform project's sprint 2026-11-08-cli-as-client ran a third whole-suite round of 16 minutes because a perf fixer changed the product after the second round had passed every test. The speed read had marked the test product-slow before that round ran.

The tests tool states each contract the faults break: one result line per test "as each finishes", a setup safe to run again, and a closing round "after the last change". The preflight ([test-preflight.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/prompts/test-preflight.md)) checks the stack's sizing alone, and `/ok-setup`'s runner check compares each kind of test with the command and the silence. Neither runs the suite command under the schedule or runs setup a second time.

Site: plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests::schedule_failures (the derived start); skills/converge/prompts/test-preflight.md and skills/ok-setup/SKILL.md section 3.7 (the checks before a sprint); skills/converge/SKILL.md step 3a.2 (the speed step on any failed round) and the fix loop's order (a perf fix after the closing round).

(2) The preflight and /ok-setup's runner check run the suite command over two tests of one held group and check the order of their lines, run testing.setup twice in a row on a running stack, and run it once beside resources it did not create. (3) A round whose failures are only schedule pairs or a failed setup files no speed step. (4) Performance improves opportunistically: certification applies a product-slow fix only when another whole-suite round will run anyway. Once a round passes with nothing left to fix, no perf fix lands after it; each remaining product-slow verdict is filed as an issue for the next sprint, which runs the full suite anyway.

messages.text: A. Move detailed test planning out of /plan-sprint and into the sprint's execution, so the owner does not wait on it. The sprint plan's test section stays high level: which stories need new tests, revised tests, or retired tests, and what the runtime tests are updated to. Any question detailed test planning raises is filed as a call or an issue at the end of the sprint, never asked mid-sprint. Time controls keep working: the check that every timing has an event control and that every timing is configurable becomes an addendum to the code plan. The test planners, or agents that do only that check, run ahead of the build during the sprint, so the build tasks build the time controls they find.

options.label: A
options.text: /plan-sprint keeps a high-level test scope: which stories get new, revised, or retired tests, and which runtime parts get their runtime scenarios updated. Detailed test planning runs as a stage of sprint execution. Each point that asks the owner today becomes a call or an issue listed at the end. A time-control check runs ahead of the build and adds time-control work as an addendum to the code plan.

problem: Where testing.enabled is on or frozen, /plan-sprint plans every test in detail before the owner approves the sprint (section 10 of skills/plan-sprint/SKILL.md). It runs one story planner per group, the runtime planner, sort tasks, and the budget task; one review task per planner task and a plan-wide review; and a re-plan, a fresh assembly, and a fresh runner check for each finding. The owner waits through all of it, so test planning sets how long planning takes. Code planning happens during planning so the owner can answer questions as they arise. Detailed test planning needs the owner at only four points: program questions (an entry point no story serves), test questions (a scenario whose outcome the sprint changes or removes), the runner check (the suite command cannot run a planned test), and approval of the plan. The test planners read the work items and implementation notes, not the built code, so they could run in execution ahead of the test stages. Step 8 turns each time control the test plan needs into a product-code work item before approval, and that step has to keep working wherever test planning runs.
